title: The three colors of fire
hookLine: look at a flame: the red is heat, the white is water, the black is food, and the 'fire' itself turns out to be a name
carry: name and form, one being beneath
tomorrow: food, water, heat become mind, breath, speech

cards: Light a match and look closely at the flame. It isn't one color. There's a reddish glow, a bright whitish part, and a dark edge where the stick is burning down.

Usually it's just fire, blown out before it reaches your fingers. Uddalaka, teaching his son Shvetaketu, looks at the same flame and sees yesterday's creation story, still going on, right there in the colors.

teach.h: EVERYTHING IS A BRAID OF THREE.
teach.b: Yesterday, Being became heat, water and food.

Now Uddalaka says Being entered into them as the living self, the jiva, gave them name and form, nama-rupa, and wove each one together with the other two, so that everything is a braid of three. Then he points to a fire.
The red color of fire is the form of heat. The white is the form of water. The black is the form of food, of earth.
And then something startling: so the fireness of fire has gone. The change is only a name, a matter of words. The truth is the three colors.
That's the clay line from two days ago, word for word, except now the pot is a flame.
He does the same with the sun, the moon and lightning: red, white and black in each, and sun-ness, moon-ness, lightning-ness only names. Then he mentions the old teachers.
The great householders of old knew this, he says, and so they said: nobody can now tell us anything we haven't heard or thought or known.

teach.h: RED IS HEAT, WHITE WATER, BLACK FOOD.
teach.b: Whatever they saw that was red, they knew as heat; white, as water; black, as food. Nobody's claiming this is how a modern lab would describe a flame.

teach.h: THE FIRENESS OF FIRE HAS GONE.
teach.b: And it doesn't mean the fire is fake; it still burns. Fire is a name for a form.
Hindus still use that pair, nama-rupa, name and form, for the changing surface of things, and under it, the one Being, which entered everything as the living self.

teach.h: NAME AND FORM, ONE BEING BENEATH.
teach.b: Many teachers read that as the root of a central Hindu teaching: the self in you is no stranger to the One.

how: The idea that everything is woven of a few basic strands runs through later Hindu thought, including the three gunas of Samkhya and the Gita; some scholars see Uddalaka's three colors as an early forerunner of these ideas, though the link is debated.

o: a dish cooked with three kinds of grain
a song sung on the third day of a feast
threefold: braided of heat, water and food

games.q: the three colors — tap the pairs.

s: Uddalaka says each thing is a braid of all three
Being wove heat, water and food together, so everything is threefold.
the text claims to describe the flame like a modern lab
it's a way of seeing: names on top, a few simple strands beneath.
he applies the three colors to the sun, the moon and lightning too
red, white and black in each; the rest is a name.

games.q: you're one of the great householders of old. you've understood the three colors. someone offers to teach you something new about the world. what do you say?
o: nobody can now tell us anything we haven't heard or known.
games.why: the text says the old householders said just that: knowing the three, they could see what anything was made of.

practice: Look at a candle, a lamp or a sunlit patch of wall, or close your eyes and picture a flame. As you find each color, give it Uddalaka's meaning: red, heat; white, water; dark, food.
Then close your eyes and rest in the afterglow, three strands and one flame.

wordCard.voice: Trivrit, threefold, braided of three. Red for heat, white for water, black for food: Uddalaka's way of seeing every fire, sun and moon this way.

orig.note: Sanskrit trivṛt: threefold, braided of three. Being made each element trivṛt.

carryVoice: Your line: name and form, one Being beneath. Three strands, and the living self in all of them. Day three hundred forty-two, done.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.3.2–4 (entering with the living self; name and form; threefold)
Chandogya Upanishad 6.4.1–7 (red, white, black; the fireness of fire gone; the old householders)
